citations.quote: All processes using a database must be on the same host computer; WAL does not work over a network filesystem. This is because WAL requires all processes to share a small amount of memory and processes on separate host machines obviously cannot share memory with each other.

claims.claim_text: Being on the same host is enough to guarantee that WAL will work.
claims.reasoning: The passages show that same-host placement alone is not sufficient: with NORMAL locking mode at the first WAL-mode access, the shared-memory wal-index is created and the underlying VFS must support the version-2 shared-memory methods, otherwise opening or converting the database fails. Passage [3] likewise notes that legacy VFSes lack these methods, so additional conditions beyond co-location apply.

citations.quote: If NORMAL locking mode is in effect for the first WAL-mode database access, then the shared-memory wal-index is created. This means that the underlying VFS must support the "version 2" shared-memory. If the VFS does not support shared-memory methods, then the attempt to open a database that is already in WAL mode, or the attempt to convert a database into WAL mode, will fail.

This feature allows WAL databases to be created, read, and written by legacy VFSes that lack the "version 2" shared-memory methods xShmMap, xShmLock, xShmBarrier, and xShmUnmap on the sqlite3_io_methods object.

citations.quote: Writers sync the WAL on every transaction commit if PRAGMA synchronous is set to FULL but omit this sync if PRAGMA synchronous is set to NORMAL.
